sections.text:
Keeping Fit in Brackenford: Five Options Compared

A. Riverside Leisure Centre is run by the town council and is the obvious choice for anyone who wants to swim as well as train. Alongside a 25-metre pool, it has a reasonably equipped gym, a sports hall and changing rooms that were completely rebuilt last year. There is no contract: you can either pay for each visit or buy a monthly pass, which can be cancelled at any time. Residents who bring a council tax bill or another proof of address receive a third off the standard price, so it is worth sorting out your paperwork before you go. The downside is that the centre gets very crowded between five and seven on weekday evenings, when queues form for the most popular machines. If your schedule allows it, mid-morning or the hour before closing is far more pleasant. Swimming lessons for children are popular and tend to fill up within days of being announced.

B. Ironworks Strength Club, tucked behind the railway station, is a very different place. Its owner, Dorothea Pemberton, competed in weightlifting for over a decade, and the club is aimed squarely at people who want to lift heavy weights rather than run on treadmills; there are only two cardio machines in the whole building. Members receive an electronic key that lets them in around the clock, but nobody is given one until they have completed a one-hour induction with a member of staff. Pemberton insists that beginners are welcome and says many of her current members had never touched a barbell before joining. Membership is charged monthly, with a minimum commitment of three months. Apart from a free technique session on Saturday mornings, there are no group classes. The changing facilities are basic, so some members shower at home.

C. If you travel a lot for work, Pulse Fitness may suit you best. It belongs to a national chain, and a standard membership gives access to more than eighty branches across the country, not just the one on the top floor of the Brackenford shopping centre. The gym floor is large and modern, and the price includes around forty classes a week, from cycling to boxing-style workouts. Members can park free for up to two hours in the shopping centre car park. However, joining usually means signing a twelve-month contract, and leaving early is expensive. There is normally a joining fee as well, although this is waived for anyone who signs up in January. Some members complain that the most popular classes are fully booked within minutes of opening for reservations.

D. Willow Studio offers no gym equipment at all; instead, it specialises in yoga and Pilates. Classes are limited to twelve people, so instructors can correct each participant's posture, and the studio is particularly popular with people who sit at a desk all day. It is run by Anselm Wiradja, a former physiotherapist, who designs a gentle beginners' course every term. Places must be booked through the studio's app, and anyone who cancels less than twelve hours before a class is charged in full. Newcomers can try one class without paying, which is a sensible way to find out whether the atmosphere suits you. Rather than a membership, you buy packs of five or ten classes, which remain valid for six months.

E. Finally, the Harbour Road Community Gym is a charity run largely by volunteers. Its equipment is older and the space is small, but it has a warm, unhurried atmosphere that appeals especially to older adults and people returning to exercise after illness or injury. Every Tuesday and Thursday, Nkechi Halvorsen, a retired nurse, leads a supervised session for anyone who feels nervous about training alone. Fees are based on what members can afford: those on a low income or receiving benefits pay a reduced rate, and nobody is asked to prove their earnings. The gym opens only on weekday mornings and two evenings a week, and it closes completely for the first two weeks of August while volunteers carry out repairs. For those willing to work around these hours, it offers remarkable value.

sections.text:
Taking On Your First Employee

A. Hiring your first member of staff is one of the biggest steps a small business owner will take. Overnight, you stop being responsible only for yourself and become responsible for someone else's income, safety and working conditions. This guide from the Eastbrook Business Advice Office sets out the main tasks involved and the order in which to tackle them. It is not a substitute for professional legal advice, and because employment rules differ from one country to another, you should always check the details that apply where you trade. Our advisers offer free one-to-one sessions every Tuesday morning for anyone who wants to talk through their plans.

B. Before you write an advertisement, ask yourself whether you genuinely need an employee. If the extra work comes in short bursts, a freelancer paid by the job may be a cheaper and more flexible solution. If you decide that a permanent role makes sense, put together a job description that sets out the main duties, the expected hours and the rate of pay. This document will shape your advertisement, guide your interviews and later form the basis of the contract, so it is worth taking time over it. Then work out what the post will really cost. Wages are only part of the picture: you may also have to pay employer contributions to the state, fund paid holidays and buy equipment or uniforms. Marguerite Oyelowo, who has advised local firms at our office for over a decade, tells clients to add about a fifth to the basic wage when they draw up their budget. 'Owners who plan around the wage alone are often caught out by the extra costs within the first few months,' she says.

C. Once the budget is settled, deal with the official side. In many countries you must register as an employer with the tax authority before the first payday, because you will be responsible for deducting income tax from your employee's wages and passing it on. You will also need a way of running payroll; many small firms use inexpensive software, while others pay an accountant to handle it. Also find out whether the law requires you to hold insurance that covers claims from staff who are injured or fall ill because of their work. In some places this cover is compulsory from the day your first employee starts, and the fines for not having it can be heavy.

D. With the paperwork under way, you can start recruiting. Advertise in places your candidate is likely to look, and ask every applicant the same core questions at interview so that you can compare them fairly. Before making a firm offer, check that your chosen candidate has the legal right to work in the country. This usually means seeing original documents, such as a passport, in the person's presence and keeping a dated copy on file. Photocopies or photographs sent by email are not enough. It is also sensible to contact at least one previous employer for a reference, although a reference should never replace your own judgement.

E. Your new employee is entitled to clear written terms. In many countries these must be provided on or before their first day, not weeks later once they have settled in. As a minimum, the document should state the job title, pay, working hours, holiday entitlement and how much notice either side must give to end the arrangement. If you include a probation period, say how long it lasts and what will happen at the end of it.

F. The first week deserves careful planning. A proper induction should cover health and safety procedures, the location of first-aid equipment, how to deal with customers and, above all, whom to ask when something is unclear. Sanjay Whitlock, who runs a bakery on Mill Street, admits he got this wrong. 'My first assistant was simply handed an apron and told to get on with it,' he recalls. 'She left after three weeks.' Since then he has used a one-page checklist for every new starter, and his second recruit has now been with him for four years.

G. Finally, keep accurate records of the hours your employee works, the pay they receive and any holiday they take, as you may be asked to produce these. Arrange a short review at the end of the probation period, and after that make time for regular conversations rather than waiting for problems to build up. Staff who feel listened to are more likely to stay, and replacing someone usually costs more than keeping them.

explanation.en: Paragraph D clearly states that photographs sent by email are not enough; the original documents must be seen in person.

explanation.uk: В абзаці D прямо сказано, що фотографій, надісланих електронною поштою, недостатньо: оригінали документів треба побачити особисто.

questions.prompt: Most job applicants provide references from more than one previous employer.

explanation.en: Paragraph D advises contacting at least one previous employer for a reference, but it says nothing about how many references applicants usually provide.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D советуют обратиться за рекомендацией хотя бы к одному из прежних работодателей, но ничего не сказано о том, сколько рекомендаций обычно предоставляют кандидаты.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D радять звернутися по рекомендацію принаймні до одного з попередніх роботодавців, але нічого не сказано про те, скільки рекомендацій зазвичай надають кандидати.

questions.prompt: The guide advises against waiting several weeks before giving a new employee written terms.
questions.evidence: on or before their first day, not weeks later once they have settled in

explanation.en: Paragraph E says written terms should be given on or before the first day, not weeks later, which matches the statement.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что письменные условия работы нужно выдать в первый день или раньше, а не через несколько недель, — это совпадает с утверждением.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що письмові умови роботи треба надати в перший день або раніше, а не через кілька тижнів, — це збігається з твердженням.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage? Write TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if the statement contradicts the information, or NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

sections.text:
Growing Together

A. On a corner of Harwick Street, where a burnt-out shop once stood, there are now raised beds of beans, a bench made from old scaffolding boards and a hand-painted sign inviting passers-by to come in. Ten years ago the site was fenced off and littered with broken glass; today around forty households share it. Scenes like this have become increasingly common. In towns and cities across many countries, neglected corners of land are being turned into community gardens – spaces where neighbours grow food and flowers side by side rather than behind their own fences. Councils that once regarded such sites as eyesores are, in some cases, now actively offering them to residents' groups. Waiting lists for a plot can run to several years in some places, a sign of how far demand has outstripped supply.

B. It would be wrong, however, to see this as a purely modern trend. During both world wars, governments in Britain and the United States urged citizens to dig up lawns, parks and even sports grounds to grow vegetables, and millions responded. Much later, in the 1970s, residents of some American cities began clearing rubbish from abandoned lots and planting them, often without asking anyone's permission. Some of those early plots still exist today, surrounded by expensive apartment blocks. What has changed is the motivation. Wartime gardeners grew food because they had to; most of today's volunteers could easily buy their carrots at the supermarket, and many admit that their home-grown ones end up costing far more. So why do they bother?

C. Kavita Ellingsen, a social researcher who spent two years visiting gardens in three cities, believes the answer has less to do with vegetables than with company. In her study, which involved interviews with more than 200 members, only a small minority named fresh food as their main reason for joining. Far more mentioned meeting neighbours, escaping loneliness or simply having somewhere to go. 'People told me again and again that they came for the tomatoes and stayed for the conversations,' she says. Ellingsen found that older members in particular valued the garden as a place where friendships formed naturally, without the awkwardness of an organised social event. She is careful to point out, though, that her study looked only at people who had already joined, so it cannot say whether gardening itself makes people less lonely.

D. Keeping a shared garden running smoothly takes more organisation than visitors might expect. Lucia Brannigan, who coordinates the Harwick Street site, explains that every member signs a short agreement before receiving a plot. It sets out simple rules: no chemical weedkillers, no planting of trees that will shade other beds, and a commitment to spend at least two hours a month on shared tasks such as turning the compost or repairing paths. Watering is organised through a rota posted on the door of the tool shed, so that nobody's crops die while their owner is on holiday. Newcomers are usually given a smaller bed for their first season, to see whether they can keep up with it. Members who repeatedly ignore the rules can eventually be asked to give up their plot, though she says this has happened only twice. 'The rules sound strict,' Brannigan admits, 'but they actually prevent arguments. When everyone knows what's expected, there's very little to fall out about.'

E. Not every garden enjoys such a stable existence. Many are created on land that is only borrowed, sometimes from a council and sometimes from a private owner waiting for the right moment to build. When that moment comes, years of work can disappear within weeks. Brannigan's own group came close to losing its site when the owner received an offer from a developer; it survived only after members raised enough money to buy a long lease. Brannigan estimates that the campaign took eighteen months and involved almost every member. Other risks are less dramatic but just as serious. Gardens often depend on a handful of committed volunteers, and when those people move away or grow tired, enthusiasm can quickly fade. There can also be friction between long-standing members, who may resist change, and newcomers with fresh ideas about what the garden should be.

F. For anyone thinking of getting involved, Marcus Tembo, a retired bus driver who has belonged to the Harwick Street garden since it opened, has some straightforward advice. Start small, he says: a single bed tended well is more satisfying than a large plot overgrown with weeds. Ask experienced members questions, since most are delighted to share what they know. And don't expect to save money – seeds, tools and the occasional failed crop add up. 'If you want cheap vegetables, go to the market,' he laughs. 'You come here for something you can't buy.' Most importantly, he adds, turn up regularly, even when there is little to do: the conversations by the compost heap matter as much as the harvest.
sections.title: Growing Together

options.text: Agreed rules that keep a shared space running
The lessons of wartime food shortages
A transformed corner reflects a growing movement
Why growing your own is cheaper than shopping
Social connection as the real attraction
A familiar practice driven by new reasons
Threats to a garden's survival
Measuring the health benefits of gardening
Practical tips from a long-serving member

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: neglected corners of land are being turned into community gardens

explanation.en: Paragraph A describes one former shop site that is now a garden and then says such changes are happening in many towns and cities, with demand growing. So the main idea is one changed place that shows a wider trend.
explanation.ru: Абзац A описывает одно бывшее помещение магазина, на месте которого теперь сад, а затем говорит, что такие перемены происходят во многих городах и спрос растёт. Значит, главная мысль — одно изменившееся место, которое отражает более широкую тенденцию.
explanation.uk: Абзац A описує одне колишнє приміщення магазину, на місці якого тепер сад, а далі говорить, що такі зміни відбуваються в багатьох містах і попит зростає. Отже, головна думка — одне змінене місце, яке ілюструє ширшу тенденцію.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: It would be wrong, however, to see this as a purely modern trend.

explanation.en: Paragraph B shows that community gardening existed in the world wars and the 1970s, but says 'What has changed is the motivation'. The wartime heading only covers one detail, and the paragraph does not discuss lessons from food shortages.
explanation.ru: Абзац B показывает, что общественные сады существовали во время мировых войн и в 1970-е годы, но там сказано: «What has changed is the motivation». Заголовок про военное время охватывает лишь одну деталь, а об уроках нехватки продовольствия в абзаце речи не идёт.
explanation.uk: Абзац B показує, що громадські сади існували під час світових воєн і в 1970-х роках, але там сказано: «What has changed is the motivation». Заголовок про воєнний час стосується лише однієї деталі, а про уроки нестачі продовольства в абзаці не йдеться.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: believes the answer has less to do with vegetables than with company

explanation.en: Paragraph C reports Ellingsen's finding that most members join to meet people rather than for food. It is about social reasons, not about measuring health, so the health heading is wrong.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C приводится вывод, к которому пришла Ellingsen: большинство участников вступают, чтобы общаться с людьми, а не ради еды. Речь идёт о социальных причинах, а не об измерении здоровья, поэтому заголовок про здоровье не подходит.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C наведено висновок, до якого дійшла Ellingsen: більшість учасників приєднуються, щоб спілкуватися з людьми, а не заради їжі. Ідеться про соціальні причини, а не про вимірювання здоров'я, тому заголовок про здоров'я не підходить.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Keeping a shared garden running smoothly takes more organisation than visitors might expect.

explanation.en: Paragraph D explains the members' agreement, the watering rota and what happens when rules are broken, and Brannigan says the rules prevent arguments. The whole paragraph is about how rules keep the garden working.
explanation.ru: Абзац D объясняет соглашение участников, график полива и то, что происходит при нарушении правил, а Brannigan говорит, что правила предотвращают ссоры. Весь абзац о том, как правила обеспечивают работу сада.
explanation.uk: Абзац D пояснює угоду учасників, графік поливу і те, що відбувається в разі порушення правил, а Brannigan каже, що правила запобігають сваркам. Увесь абзац про те, як правила забезпечують роботу саду.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: Not every garden enjoys such a stable existence.

explanation.en: Paragraph E lists dangers: losing borrowed land to builders, volunteers getting tired, and friction between members. All of these threaten whether a garden can continue.
explanation.ru: Абзац E перечисляет угрозы: потерю земли, взятой во временное пользование, из-за застройщиков, усталость волонтёров и трения между участниками. Всё это ставит под вопрос, сможет ли сад продолжать существовать.
explanation.uk: Абзац E перелічує небезпеки: втрату землі, взятої в тимчасове користування, через забудовників, утому волонтерів і тертя між учасниками. Усе це ставить під загрозу подальше існування саду.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: a retired bus driver who has belonged to the Harwick Street garden since it opened, has some straightforward advice

explanation.en: Paragraph F gives Tembo's advice to beginners: start small, ask questions and come regularly. The heading about saving money is wrong because Tembo says gardeners should not expect to save money.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F приводятся советы Tembo новичкам: начинать с малого, задавать вопросы и приходить регулярно. Заголовок про экономию денег не подходит, потому что Tembo говорит, что садоводам не стоит рассчитывать на экономию.
explanation.uk: В абзаці F наведено поради Tembo новачкам: починати з малого, ставити запитання й приходити регулярно. Заголовок про економію грошей не підходить, бо Tembo каже, що садівникам не варто розраховувати на економію.

groups.instruction: The reading passage has six paragraphs, A–F. Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below. There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use them all.

questions.prompt: In the 1970s, some residents of American cities cultivated abandoned lots, frequently without seeking ______.
questions.evidence: often without asking anyone's permission

explanation.en: Paragraph B says these residents planted abandoned lots 'often without asking anyone's permission'. 'Frequently' restates 'often' and 'seeking' restates 'asking'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B сказано, что эти жители засаживали заброшенные участки «often without asking anyone's permission». «Frequently» передаёт «often», а «seeking» — «asking».
explanation.uk: В абзаці B сказано, що ці мешканці засаджували покинуті ділянки «often without asking anyone's permission». «Frequently» передає «often», а «seeking» — «asking».

questions.prompt: Older members especially appreciated that friendships developed without the ______ of a planned social gathering.
questions.evidence: without the awkwardness of an organised social event

explanation.en: Paragraph C says older members liked the garden because friendships formed naturally, without the awkwardness of an organised social event. 'A planned social gathering' restates 'an organised social event'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C говорится, что пожилым участникам нравился сад, потому что дружба там возникала естественно, без неловкости организованного мероприятия для общения. «A planned social gathering» — это перефразированное «an organised social event».
explanation.uk: В абзаці C йдеться про те, що літнім учасникам подобався сад, бо дружба там виникала природно, без ніяковості організованого заходу для спілкування. «A planned social gathering» — це перефразоване «an organised social event».

questions.prompt: To stop crops dying while their owners are away, a watering timetable is displayed on the ______ door.
questions.evidence: a rota posted on the door of the tool shed

explanation.en: Paragraph D says the watering rota is posted on the door of the tool shed so that crops do not die while their owner is on holiday. 'Timetable' restates 'rota'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D сказано, что график полива висит на двери сарая для инструментов, чтобы урожай не погиб, пока его хозяин в отпуске. «Timetable» — это перефразированное «rota».
explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що графік поливу висить на дверях сараю для інструментів, щоб урожай не загинув, поки його власник у відпустці. «Timetable» — це перефразоване «rota».

questions.prompt: Members joining the garden normally receive a ______ during their first season.
questions.evidence: Newcomers are usually given a smaller bed for their first season

explanation.en: Paragraph D says newcomers are usually given a smaller bed in their first season to see if they can manage it. 'Members joining' restates 'newcomers'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D говорится, что новичкам в первый сезон обычно дают грядку поменьше, чтобы проверить, справятся ли они. «Members joining» — это перефразированное «newcomers».
explanation.uk: В абзаці D йдеться про те, що новачкам у перший сезон зазвичай дають меншу грядку, щоб перевірити, чи вони впораються. «Members joining» — це перефразоване «newcomers».

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

options.text: Interest in plots has grown faster than the number available.
Many applicants give up before a plot finally becomes free.
Councils have been slow to offer unused land to residents.
Most gardens limit their membership to around forty households.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about the long waiting lists for garden plots?
questions.evidence: a sign of how far demand has outstripped supply

explanation.en: Paragraph A says the waiting lists show that demand has outstripped supply, meaning more people want plots than there are plots. The passage says some councils are now offering land, and 'forty households' refers only to Harwick Street.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A сказано, что листы ожидания показывают: спрос превысил предложение, то есть желающих получить участок больше, чем самих участков. В тексте говорится, что некоторые городские советы уже предлагают землю, а «forty households» относится только к Harwick Street.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A сказано, що списки очікування показують: попит перевищив пропозицію, тобто охочих отримати ділянку більше, ніж самих ділянок. У тексті йдеться про те, що деякі міські ради вже пропонують землю, а «forty households» стосується лише Harwick Street.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

options.text: It found older members were the loneliest of all.
It cannot establish whether gardening reduces loneliness.
It relied mainly on members who had recently left.
It covered more cities than any earlier piece of research.

questions.prompt: What does Ellingsen point out about her own study?
questions.evidence: it cannot say whether gardening itself makes people less lonely

explanation.en: In paragraph C, Ellingsen says her study only included people who had already joined, so it cannot show whether gardening itself makes people less lonely. It studied current members, not people who had left, and it does not compare older members' loneliness or mention earlier research.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C Ellingsen говорит, что в её исследование вошли только люди, которые уже вступили в сад, поэтому оно не может показать, уменьшает ли одиночество само садоводство. Исследование касалось нынешних участников, а не тех, кто ушёл; в нём не сравнивается одиночество пожилых участников и не упоминаются более ранние работы.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C Ellingsen каже, що до її дослідження увійшли лише люди, які вже приєдналися до саду, тому воно не може показати, чи саме садівництво зменшує самотність. Дослідження стосувалося теперішніх учасників, а не тих, хто пішов; у ньому не порівнюється самотність літніх учасників і не згадуються попередні роботи.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

options.text: are frequently ignored by the newer members.
were introduced after a serious dispute arose.
help to stop disagreements between the members.
are stricter than those of most similar gardens.

questions.prompt: According to Brannigan, the garden's rules
questions.evidence: they actually prevent arguments

explanation.en: In paragraph D, Brannigan says the rules sound strict but actually prevent arguments, because everyone knows what is expected. She does not compare them with other gardens, and members have been asked to leave only twice, so the rules are not often ignored.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D Brannigan говорит, что правила кажутся строгими, но на деле предотвращают ссоры, потому что все знают, чего от них ждут. Она не сравнивает их с правилами других садов, а покинуть сад участников просили всего дважды, так что правила нарушают нечасто.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D Brannigan каже, що правила здаються суворими, але насправді запобігають сваркам, бо всі знають, чого від них очікують. Вона не порівнює їх із правилами інших садів, а залишити сад учасників просили лише двічі, тож правила порушують нечасто.
